chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

data.Proposed: Saudi-funded port, airport, desalination plant, electrical grid

dyk: … that the Saudi-administered Gaza plan floated in the Israeli press was first proposed in 1991, when [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) was a first-tour officer in [Saudi Arabia](/wiki/saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry) — and Israel answered *"absolutely never"*?

… that before [October 7](/wiki/october-7-attack), [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says [Gaza](/wiki/st-porphyrios-church-gaza) had about five hours of water a day and a few hours of electricity before Israel switched each off?
chas-freeman-gaza-plan-1991.body:
The **1991 Saudi plan for Gaza** is [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou)'s account of an infrastructure proposal made during his first overseas posting, which he raises whenever a version of it resurfaces.

In 1991 Kiriakou was a new [CIA](/wiki/cia) officer on his first overseas tour, in Saudi Arabia, working to an ambassador he describes as having become legendary — Chas Freeman, later ambassador to China and an assistant secretary of defense, *"brilliant"* in Kiriakou's assessment.<Cite t="29:03" /> Freeman put a question to the Saudis: what if they were asked to build a port, an airport, a water desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza? *"And they said, yeah, we would do it."*<Cite t="29:03" /> The proposal was then taken to the Israelis, *"and the Israelis said, absolutely never."*<Cite t="29:35" />

Kiriakou raises the episode because the same architecture reappeared in the Israeli press more than three decades later: Israel would technically continue to own Gaza while day-to-day administration passed to Saudi Arabia, which would also invest in an electrical grid, desalination, and a port, with Gaza disarmed and no Palestinian military. He calls it *"a great idea"* — and notes he has said so on podcasts more than once — before adding the date: *"That was 1991."*<Cite t="28:31" /><Cite t="29:03" />

## Why he thinks the question recurs

The reason Kiriakou keeps returning to the plan is his reading of the conditions it was meant to relieve. Before [October 7](/wiki/october-7-attack), he says, Gaza had *"but 5 hours of water every day"* before Israel shut it off, and a few hours of electricity before Israel shut that off too.<Cite t="29:35" /> His conclusion is stated as a prediction rather than a judgement: *"The situation's untenable because another October 7th is going to happen if there's not a sort of a pressure release valve."*<Cite t="29:35" /> He closes the thought with a line he attributes to Martin Luther King: *"Never underestimate a man's desire to be free."*<Cite t="30:07" />

On the ceasefire that had just been reached at the time of the interview, Kiriakou is careful about the word: *"It's not a peace deal. It's just a ceasefire. It doesn't address a single one of the core issues. Not a single one."*<Cite t="26:27" /> He says he is rooting for it to hold, and commends the populations on both sides for trying, while withholding any confidence in either leadership — and states that a durable settlement requires an independent Palestine, *"because the current situation's untenable."*<Cite t="26:57" /><Cite t="28:01" />

king-abdullah-ii.title: King Abdullah II of Jordan
king-abdullah-ii.summary: The Jordanian monarch whom John Kiriakou rates as knowing more about the Middle East than anyone else who leads or studies it, and as almost never wrong across twenty-five years of foreign-policy predictions. Kiriakou recounts the deathbed succession that made him king against his own expectations, and his refusal after October 7 to accept Palestinian refugees on the grounds that doing so would deliver Israel the ethnic cleansing it wanted.

data.Became crown prince: Weeks before his father's death, replacing his uncle
data.Per Kiriakou: Knows the region better than anyone; 'almost never wrong'
data.On Palestinian refugees: Refused — would hand Israel the ethnic cleansing it wants

dyk: … that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says [King Abdullah II](/wiki/king-abdullah-ii) refused to take Palestinian refugees after [October 7](/wiki/october-7-attack) precisely because he did *not* want to hand Israel an ethnic cleansing — even though his own wife is Palestinian?

… that [King Abdullah II](/wiki/king-abdullah-ii) became crown prince only weeks before his father died, after King Hussein sacked his own brother for restaffing the Joint Chiefs of Staff too early — a story [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says he heard while stationed in [Athens](/wiki/greek-intelligence-service)?
king-abdullah-ii.body:
**King Abdullah II of Jordan** is, in [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou)'s assessment, the best-informed head of state in the Middle East. Asked about the king's record, Kiriakou goes further than his interviewer: *"I would go so far as to say of everybody in the region or everybody who studies the region, no one knows as much as King Abdullah,"* and describes him as almost never wrong across twenty-five years of foreign-policy predictions.<Cite t="43:49" /> He calls him *"the right leader for that country."*<Cite t="43:49" />

## The succession

Kiriakou's account of how Abdullah got the throne turns on a misjudgement by someone else. King Hussein was dying slowly of cancer and was, in Kiriakou's phrase, universally loved — he recalls that his own wife wept at the news while they were stationed in [Athens](/wiki/greek-intelligence-service).<Cite t="44:51" /> As the king approached death, the crown prince — Hussein's brother — began making preliminary changes, including restaffing the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Hussein's response, as Kiriakou renders it: *"Whoa, I'm not even dead yet. We're not going to do this. You're fired."* Abdullah was named crown prince in his place and, on Kiriakou's telling, was as surprised as anyone: *"What? I never wanted to be crown prince."* His father died a couple of months later.<Cite t="45:22" />

## After October 7

Asked at a conference in the weeks after 7 October 2023 whether Jordan would accept Palestinian refugees, Abdullah answered — in Kiriakou's account — that he was glad to be asked, and that he would not. The reason he gave was not reluctance: *"Not because I don't want them, not because I don't like them. My wife is Palestinian."* It was that acceptance would settle the question in Israel's favour — *"If I do accept them though, I will give Israel exactly what they want. They will be able to ethnically cleanse the whole area."*<Cite t="45:53" /> Kiriakou pairs the answer with a later image of the king seated beside [Donald Trump](/wiki/donald-trump) in the Oval Office while Trump discussed moving Palestinians into Jordan.<Cite t="46:25" /> His own verdict on that prospect is flat: *"Not going to happen. It's just not."*<Cite t="46:25" />

## Why Jordan says no

Kiriakou grounds the refusal in Jordanian memory rather than sentiment. In 1968, he says, the Jordanian military was fighting Palestinians on the steps of the palace as Black September attempted to murder King Hussein and his family and turn the country into Palestine — *"and they have long memories in Jordan."*<Cite t="38:02" /> Half the population is Palestinian, the children and grandchildren of 1948 refugees, as is half the royal couple; but, he says, they will never be fully Jordanian. He points to the documents as the proof: Jordanians carry a green passport, and *"if you're Palestinian born in Jordan, you carry a black passport."*<Cite t="38:34" /> The generalisation he draws is broader — governments across the Middle East *"say the right things about Palestinians, but when it comes time to put their money where their mouths are, not a whole lot gets done."*<Cite t="39:06" />

cia-france-rift-1990s.title: The CIA–France rift of the 1990s
cia-france-rift-1990s.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a period in the early 1990s when a caught CIA officer in Paris triggered mass expulsions and a standing order barring agency officers from even transiting Charles de Gaulle airport — including a colleague's secure laptop being destroyed on a railroad spike, an attempted moving-car pickup of Kiriakou himself in Pakistan, and his assessment that French intelligence is both exceptionally talented and willing to kill.

data.Trigger: A first-tour CIA officer caught pushing too far
data.Response: Expulsion of the officer, the chief of station and others
data.Consequence: Officers barred from transiting Charles de Gaulle airport

dyk: … that after a [CIA](/wiki/cia) officer was caught in Paris, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says agency officers were barred from even changing planes at Charles de Gaulle — and that French officers had driven a railroad spike through a colleague's secure laptop?

… that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says a French intelligence officer in [Pakistan](/wiki/pakistan-station-2002) tried to run tradecraft on him with a moving-car pickup — and that he refused, telling him *"you're not recruiting me"*?
cia-france-rift-1990s.body:
The **CIA–France rift of the 1990s** is [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou)'s account of a rupture between two nominally allied services, and of why he regards French intelligence as among the most capable and least restrained in the world.

## The expulsions

The cause, Kiriakou says, was one of the agency's own: *"one of our young junior first tour guys got caught just going pushing a little too far."* He accepts the French were entitled to be angry — *"deservedly so"* — but not the scale of the response. France expelled the officer, the chief of station, *"and a whole bunch of people,"* and the relationship stayed difficult for three or four years.<Cite t="1:47:41" />

What followed was a retaliation of a more bureaucratic kind. A colleague travelling on a diplomatic passport to Africa, which then meant connecting through Paris, was ordered to switch on and open his secure laptop. He refused, citing his passport and the property of the U.S. Department of State. French officers took the machine into a back room, where — as Kiriakou relays it — they had a railroad spike fastened to a table and *"just slammed it down on the railroad spike, went all the way through the laptop,"* then pulled it off and handed it back.<Cite t="1:48:42" /> Headquarters' answer was a standing prohibition: nobody could transit Charles de Gaulle airport any more — which, Kiriakou notes, had been the only reason he was ever in France, catching connections to the Middle East.<Cite t="1:48:11" /><Cite t="1:48:42" />

## The attempted pickup

Kiriakou's own encounter came in [Pakistan](/wiki/pakistan-station-2002), where he met foreign intelligence officers almost daily to trade information — *"hey, I heard there's a safe house over here."*<Cite t="1:49:13" /> A French officer asked to meet him not at a restaurant but on a specified corner in a residential neighbourhood. The car came down the street, turned, and the door was opened from the inside: *"Get in."* Kiriakou refused, telling him there was a term of art for that kind of pickup: *"I don't work for you and you're not using tradecraft on me… No, no, no, no. You're not recruiting me."* He offered coffee at a hotel restaurant instead, and never saw the man again.<Cite t="1:49:43" /><Cite t="1:50:14" />

## His assessment of the service

Kiriakou rates French intelligence as genuinely formidable — *"they're very talented"* — and separately as willing to kill. He says French services will kill Greenpeace activists who attempt to board or deface a ship, and are operating across the Sahel, which he gives as one reason the United States has less presence there: the region's former French colonies are worked by the French, *"just killing all kinds of al-Qaeda people."*<Cite t="1:50:44" /><Cite t="1:51:15" /> He includes France, with Cuba, immediately behind Israel, China and Russia on the list of espionage threats new [CIA](/wiki/cia) officers are shown, and situates the whole relationship against the [Five Eyes](/wiki/five-eyes) arrangement: France is a NATO country and a close partner, *"but we don't give them everything like we do with the Five Eyes."*<Cite t="1:47:09" /><Cite t="1:55:24" />

## Diana

Asked whether French intelligence must know what happened when Diana, Princess of Wales, was killed in Paris, Kiriakou says they probably do — and then declines the conclusion the question invites. His own reading is a chain of failures rather than an operation: *"I really believe it was a series of fuckups."* The driver was drunk, the paparazzi were overly aggressive, one thing led to the next; he notes she had a crushed chest and suspects she was not wearing a seatbelt. *"I don't think the royal family assassinated her."*<Cite t="1:55:56" /><Cite t="1:56:28" />

robert-jackson-federal-prosecutor-speech.title: Robert Jackson's "The Federal Prosecutor"
robert-jackson-federal-prosecutor-speech.summary: The 1940 address by Attorney General and later Supreme Court justice Robert Jackson that John Kiriakou quotes as the standard against which he measures prosecutions he would personally like to see succeed — including that of John Brennan. Its central warning is that a prosecutor who picks the man first can always find the crime afterwards.

data.Speaker: Robert Jackson, U.S. Attorney General; later Supreme Court justice and Nuremberg judge
data.Central warning: Picking the man first, then searching the law books for an offence
data.Kiriakou's use: The test he applies against his own desire to see [John Brennan](/wiki/john-brennan) prosecuted

dyk: … that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) quotes a 1940 speech by Robert Jackson against his own wish to see [John Brennan](/wiki/john-brennan) imprisoned — because it warns that a prosecutor can pick the man first and find the crime later?

… that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) pairs Jackson's warning with the line attributed to Stalin's police — *show me the man and I'll show you the crime* — when describing the [Espionage Act](/wiki/espionage-act) cases brought against people like him?
robert-jackson-federal-prosecutor-speech.body:
**"The Federal Prosecutor"** is an address by Robert Jackson, delivered while he was Attorney General of the United States and long before he became a Supreme Court justice and a judge at the Nuremberg trials, which [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) quotes as a check on his own instincts. He introduces Jackson as *"one of the most important judges we've ever had."*<Cite t="2:13:38" />

The first passage Kiriakou reads out inverts the usual account of who protects whom: *"It is not the function of government to keep the citizen from falling to error. It is the function of the citizen to keep the government from falling to error."*<Cite t="2:14:11" />

The second is the one he calls the most important thing Jackson said, and he reads it in full:

> With the law books filled with a great assortment of crimes, a prosecutor stands a fair chance of finding at least a technical violation of some act on the part of almost anyone. In such a case, it is not a question of discovering the commission of a crime and then looking for the man who has committed it. It's a question of picking the man and then searching the law books or putting investigators to work to pin some offense on him.<Cite t="2:14:41" /><Cite t="2:15:12" />

His interviewer's response — that this is *"the Stalin bar. Show me the man, I'll show you the crime"* — draws Kiriakou's agreement, along with the observation that the same argument is still being had eighty-five years later.<Cite t="2:15:12" />

## What he uses it for

Kiriakou applies the speech directly against his own preference. He says he hates [John Brennan](/wiki/john-brennan), believes Brennan committed crimes to ruin his life, and would love to see him imprisoned *"even if it was just for a day or a week, just to be dragged down into the muck like he did to me and to [Jeffrey Sterling](/wiki/jeffrey-sterling) and to Ed Snowden."*<Cite t="2:15:45" /> The next sentence is the point of quoting Jackson at all: *"On the other hand, I believe in Robert Jackson and what he said."* If Brennan has legitimately committed crimes — and Kiriakou believes he has — he should be prosecuted; but where prosecutors are *"scouring the law books looking for a crime,"* Kiriakou says he would prefer not to see it happen.<Cite t="2:16:16" /><Cite t="2:16:48" />

The same standard produces his position on the prosecutions of [Donald Trump](/wiki/donald-trump), which he calls mistakes, and his view that Joe Biden should have pardoned Trump and the Republicans under investigation as Gerald Ford pardoned Richard Nixon.<Cite t="2:19:56" /><Cite t="2:20:27" />

abraxas-corporation.title: Abraxas Corporation
abraxas-corporation.summary: A CIA-adjacent contractor whose origin John Kiriakou describes as accidental: a group of senior officers who retired around 2000 formed an LLC mainly so they could smoke cigars, play pinochle and take a tax deduction, then bid low-skill cleared-staffing contracts to keep it alive — and, because headquarters knew them all, grew into a company worth billions.

data.Founded: circa 2000, by retiring senior CIA officers
data.Original purpose (per Kiriakou): A tax deduction on cigars and coffee

dyk: … that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says the [CIA](/wiki/cia) contractor [Abraxas](/wiki/abraxas-corporation) began as an LLC set up by retired officers who mainly wanted a tax deduction on their cigars — and that they *"never expected to be billionaires"*?

… that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) calls [Abraxas](/wiki/abraxas-corporation) the *"greatest shell company of all time"*, and places it in the same revolving door he describes at [In-Q-Tel](/wiki/in-q-tel) and [Palantir](/wiki/palantir)?
abraxas-corporation.body:
**Abraxas Corporation** is a cleared-services contractor whose founding [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) offers as a case study in how money finds the intelligence business without anyone setting out to make any.

Around the time he came home from Athens in 2000 there was a wave of senior [CIA](/wiki/cia) retirements — *"the head of European operations, the head of near east operations, the head of domestic operations, whatever."* The men involved formed an LLC, on Kiriakou's account, for no operational reason at all: somewhere to *"smoke cigars and drink coffee and hang out and play pinochle all day"* and take a tax deduction against it.<Cite t="3:08:21" />

The problem was that keeping the deduction required showing a gain in two years out of five. Their solution was the lowest-effort contract available: what Kiriakou calls *"butts and seats"* work — *"you just take anybody who's got a security clearance, put them in these seats, let them do data entry for six months, and then the contract's over and they all get fired."* Because the staff were on 1099s, the churn cost the company nothing.<Cite t="3:08:52" />

## Why it grew

What converted the arrangement into a business, in Kiriakou's telling, was proximity rather than capability. He says he remembers it happening: headquarters would identify a need, and someone would say *"what about Jack? Jack's got this Abraxas thing now" — "we know everybody. They're all friends of ours."*<Cite t="3:09:23" /> His interviewer's summary — *"greatest shell company of all time"* — is one Kiriakou lets stand.<Cite t="3:09:23" />

The company reached roughly $20 billion, was taken over two or three times and changed names more than once; Kiriakou believes it still operates as Abraxas and is based in Tysons Corner, Virginia. His closing observation is about intent rather than scale: *"These guys never expected to be billionaires. They were just looking for a tax deduction on their coffee and cigars."*<Cite t="3:09:55" />

He raises the story in the middle of a longer argument about the [CIA](/wiki/cia)'s commercial entanglements — [In-Q-Tel](/wiki/in-q-tel), which he says put the agency into venture capital for profit, and [Palantir](/wiki/palantir) — as evidence that the pattern is structural rather than exceptional.<Cite t="3:00:06" /><Cite t="3:08:21" />

bahrain-dole-campaign-solicitation.title: The Bahrain campaign-contribution report
bahrain-dole-campaign-solicitation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of learning, as notetaker for the U.S. ambassador to Bahrain, that a former ambassador working for the Bob Dole campaign had solicited and received $50,000 from the Amir — an illegal foreign contribution. Instructed to leave it out of the cable, he reported it months later to the CIA general counsel anyway, was told it was a felony, and was told a year afterwards that nothing had come of it.

data.Legal status: Illegal foreign national contribution; a felony
data.Instruction received: Leave it out of the cable
data.Outcome: Reported to CIA general counsel; referred to DOJ; nothing happened

dyk: … that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says he reported a $50,000 illegal campaign contribution from the Amir of [Bahrain](/wiki/bahrain-1994-1996-posting) — and was told a year later that the Justice Department *"didn't give a shit"*?

… that the reason [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) reported it at all was the [polygraph](/wiki/kiriakou-transfer-to-operations): he feared being asked whether he knew of a crime he had not reported, which would have ended his [CIA](/wiki/cia) career?
bahrain-dole-campaign-solicitation.body:
The **Bahrain campaign-contribution report** is [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou)'s account of a felony he learned about by accident, was told to omit from the record, and reported anyway.

During his posting in [Bahrain](/wiki/bahrain-1994-1996-posting) he was frequently used as notetaker by Ambassador David Ransom — *"one of the just finest human beings I've ever worked for"* — in meetings with the Bahraini foreign minister. Ransom's habit was to flag any sensitive point during the car ride to the ministry: *"Don't let me forget to say X."*<Cite t="2:45:00" /><Cite t="2:45:32" />

At one such meeting Ransom forgot, and at the close asked Kiriakou whether anything had been missed. The item was a warning: a predecessor of Ransom's as ambassador to Bahrain was now working for the Bob Dole campaign, might come out and ask for money, and *"it is illegal for a foreign national to contribute money to an American political campaign."* The minister's reply was that the man had already been — *"we gave him $50,000. We didn't realize it was illegal"* — and that the money had come from the Amir.<Cite t="2:46:04" /><Cite t="2:46:36" />

Back in the car, Ransom gave an instruction. Cables are broken out by subject, and this one was not to appear in any of them: *"That's a hornet's nest that I don't think either one of us want to be involved in."* Kiriakou complied at the time.<Cite t="2:46:36" /><Cite t="2:47:07" />

## The report

What changed his mind, on his own account, was self-interest rather than conscience — *"for my own selfish reasons."* He thought about the episode repeatedly over the following months and arrived at the question that decided it: *"what happens if I go for my next polygraph and they ask me if I'm aware of a crime that I didn't report? Then it's me, then I get fired."*<Cite t="2:47:38" />

He telephoned the [CIA](/wiki/cia) general counsel's office cold. The lawyer who answered, on hearing his surname, asked whether he was from Farrell, Pennsylvania, and whether his father was Chris — Kiriakou's father had been best man at the lawyer's in-laws' wedding. They met for coffee in the cafeteria instead.<Cite t="2:48:10" /> Told the story, the lawyer's answer was immediate: *"Oh yeah, that's a felony."* He instructed Kiriakou to put it in an email so it could be sent to the Justice Department, on the reasoning that everyone who knew — Kiriakou, the lawyer, and the ambassador — was liable to prosecution if the department learned of it independently.<Cite t="2:48:42" />

About a year later, over one of the monthly lunches of the agency's Greek-American group, Kiriakou asked what had become of it. *"They didn't give a shit. Nothing ever happened."* His own summary of the episode is unsentimental: *"Okay, well, we did the right thing."*<Cite t="2:49:13" />

kiriakou-indian-pakistani-media-policy.title: Kiriakou's policy on Indian and Pakistani media
kiriakou-indian-pakistani-media-policy.summary: A standing rule John Kiriakou adopted after an interview with an Indian outlet was rewritten into a banner headline claiming he had revealed a secret: no further interviews to any Indian or Pakistani news organisation. The remark that triggered it — that India would defeat Pakistan in a conventional war because it has five times the population — produced more death threats than he could count, and a formal demand for an apology from Imran Khan's party.

infobox.title: Kiriakou's policy on Indian and Pakistani media

data.The rule: No interviews to any Indian or Pakistani news outlet
data.Trigger: Invented banner headline claiming a CIA revelation
data.The remark: India would win a conventional war; it has five times the people
data.Consequences: Uncounted death threats; a party demand for an apology

dyk: … that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) stopped giving interviews to [Indian](/wiki/india) and Pakistani outlets entirely after one turned a routine remark into a banner headline — and that the remark brought more death threats than he could count?

… that when [Imran Khan](/wiki/imran-khan)'s party formally demanded an apology from [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou), his lawyer told him to bin the letter and he replied to it instead — noting the party had omitted that its leader was in prison?
kiriakou-indian-pakistani-media-policy.body:
**Kiriakou's policy on Indian and Pakistani media** is a blanket rule [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) announced in November 2025: *"no more interviews to any Indian or Pakistani news outlets ever again."* He prefaced it by conceding it would cause him trouble to say so.<Cite t="2:32:26" />

The reason he gives is not the content of the questions but the treatment of the answers. He says he said nothing in the interview that he had not said a thousand times, and that he had stated the caveat he always states — *"I told you my information's 25 years old"* — but that the outlet ran it under an invented banner headline with two exclamation points announcing that a CIA officer had finally revealed the truth. *"They just make shit up."*<Cite t="2:32:26" /><Cite t="2:32:58" />

## The remark

The substance was a single sentence: that in a conventional conflict [India](/wiki/india) would beat [Pakistan](/wiki/pakistan-islam-economic-critique) because it has five times the people. He elaborates the reasoning elsewhere in the same conversation — that Bangladesh and Afghanistan both align with India against Pakistan, leaving Pakistan *"outmanned and surrounded by your enemies"* — and traces the hostility to the two countries having once been one, partitioned in 1947, with Bangladesh separating from East Pakistan in 1971.<Cite t="2:35:06" /><Cite t="2:36:09" /> His account of why the two are so hostile is characteristically blunt: *"because they're exactly alike."*<Cite t="2:35:06" />

The response was death threats — *"I've lost count of how many death threats I received"* — and advice from his lawyer to keep a low profile and be aware of his surroundings.<Cite t="2:32:58" /><Cite t="2:33:30" />

## The letter

He then received a letter from the president of [Imran Khan](/wiki/imran-khan)'s political party condemning the remark in the strongest possible terms and demanding an immediate apology to the former prime minister, to the party's members, and to the people of Pakistan. His lawyer told him to throw it away. He did not: he emailed a reply consisting, in his account, of the sentence *"in regards to your demand for an apology, I wipe my ass with your demands for an apology,"* and heard nothing further.<Cite t="2:33:30" /><Cite t="2:34:02" />

He notes two consequences. The first, per his lawyer, is that a standing invitation to speak at the Pakistani military academy is now void — *"I'll never go back ever again."*<Cite t="2:34:34" /> The second is an observation about the letter itself: the party president *"neglected to say in the letter that his prime minister is in prison right now,"* running the party from his cell.<Cite t="2:36:40" />

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Whispers in the Dirt
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: John Kiriakou's second cemetery book — a guide to the mafia graves of New York City, and the sequel Simon & Schuster commissioned after Remains of the Day. Reporting it produced the moment he realised an inmate who had told him a body was found in a barrel in his storage unit had been telling the truth.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.body:
**Whispers in the Dirt: A Definitive Guide to the Mafia Graves of New York City** is the second of [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou)'s cemetery books, following [Remains of the Day](/wiki/remains-of-the-day-book). In November 2025 he described it as about seventy percent complete and due with his editor by the end of the year.<Cite t="1:17:35" /><Cite t="1:18:06" />

The book is organised cemetery by cemetery — Kiriakou lists St. Stephen's and Holy Cross among those *"just overflowing with mob guys"*, going back to Joe the Boss Masseria, the Clutch Hand, and Lucky Luciano, whose private mausoleum he calls magnificent.<Cite t="1:20:44" /> A closing chapter covers what he calls non-traditional burial grounds: the Gowanus Canal, *"where they're pulling bodies out of all the time"*; a vacant lot in the Bronx known locally as the mafia graveyard; and the Meadowlands.<Cite t="1:20:44" /><Cite t="1:21:16" />

## The body in the barrel

The episode Kiriakou uses to explain the book's appeal began in prison. He had asked one of the mafia inmates what he was in for, and got an answer he took as deflection: they found a body in a barrel in his storage unit, he did not know how it got there, and a hundred people had access to the unit. Kiriakou laughed it off with *"no judgment from me. I was just curious."*<Cite t="1:18:38" />

Years later, photographing graves in the Bronx with his girlfriend, he could not place the man whose headstone he needed. Pulling up his own manuscript, he read the entry: the victim had been a driver, initially assumed to be the hitman in his boss's killing because he could not be found, and discovered six months later in a barrel in a storage unit in New Jersey. *"Oh my god. It was the first time I put it together. It's the body from the barrel."*<Cite t="1:19:10" />

The manuscript also contained the part the inmate had left out: the driver had been too tall to fit in the barrel and was cut in half, and the barrel was full of glue, which took the coroner roughly four months to remove before an autopsy could be performed. The remains were reassembled for burial. Kiriakou's conclusion was about the inmate rather than the crime: *"Oh, dang. He was telling me the truth."*<Cite t="1:19:42" /><Cite t="1:20:13" /> He does not use the man's name in the book, on the grounds that he is out of prison.<Cite t="1:20:13" />

greek-death-rituals.title: Greek death rituals
greek-death-rituals.summary: The five-year grave rental, exhumation and ossuary practice of rural Greece as John Kiriakou describes it — bones washed in red wine, blessed, boxed, and eventually laid beneath the foundations of a new church, with cremation strictly forbidden. He visits the ossuary in his ancestral Rhodes village, where the records stop in the nineteenth century because the Ottomans burned everything earlier.

data.Practice: Grave rented for five years, then exhumation

data.Final resting place: Beneath the foundations of a new church

dyk: … that in the [Greek death rituals](/wiki/greek-death-rituals) [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) describes, a body not yet reduced to bone after five years is understood to mean the deceased went to hell — and is put straight back in the ground?

… that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) found a relative in an ossuary on [Rhodes](/wiki/rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story) — a priest executed by the Ottomans for teaching children Greek, whose death his grandmother had always described as a shark attack?
greek-death-rituals.body:
**Greek death rituals**, as [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) describes them, follow from a constraint of geography rather than of theology. Only about two percent of Greece is arable, and the good land is needed to grow food, so there are almost no cemeteries in the country in the sense understood elsewhere. Instead a grave is rented for five years.<Cite t="1:32:38" /> His source is a book he found at a flea market or secondhand bookshop, *Death Rituals of Rural Greece*.<Cite t="1:32:38" />

Because the Greek practice does not embalm, the body is placed in the ground for five years and then, on the fifth anniversary of the burial, exhumed by the women of the village together with the village priest. Kiriakou notes the test embedded in the rite: by then the remains should be a skeleton, and *"if you're not just a skeleton by then, that means you went to hell"* — in which case the body goes back in the ground.<Cite t="1:33:11" />

The skeleton is taken apart, washed with red wine, blessed by the priest, and placed in a small bone box in an ossuary — a bone house — where the boxes sit on shelves. When a new church is built, the bones are taken out and laid beneath its foundations. Asked why cremation is not simply used instead, Kiriakou is definite: *"cremation's forbidden. Strictly forbidden."* Neither he nor his interviewer finds a religious basis for the distinction; his own view is that *"some guy one day had a bright idea and said, this is what we're going to do now as a religion."*<Cite t="1:33:43" /><Cite t="1:34:13" /><Cite t="1:34:43" />

## The ossuary on Rhodes

Kiriakou visits the ossuary in his family's village whenever he returns to [Rhodes](/wiki/rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story). Its keeper is a man he has struck up a friendship with, who — in Kiriakou's careful phrasing, *"the nice way of saying it these days is he's on the spectrum"* — is unable to care for himself and was given the bone house to look after as a job. He lets Kiriakou go through the boxes looking for grandparents and great-grandparents; when he finds one, he photographs the box, opens it, and *"give[s] them a kiss on the skull."*<Cite t="1:35:14" />

Beneath the ossuary floor is a trapdoor and a space that goes back to the nineteenth century, and no further: *"The Turks burned all of our records, so we don't know really anything about where we come from."*<Cite t="1:35:45" />

In an ossuary on the southern tip of the island he found his great-great-grandfather's brother, a priest, kept above ground rather than buried beneath the church. The family account of his death was that he had been diving for sponges and eaten by a shark; a cousin who shares Kiriakou's interest in the family genealogy told him it was not true. The Ottoman authorities had executed him for teaching children to speak Greek during the occupation, and thrown his body into the sea, where sharks ate it.<Cite t="1:36:17" /><Cite t="1:36:48" /><Cite t="1:37:20" />

## Cemeteries generally

Kiriakou goes to cemeteries at least weekly, and almost daily when he is overseas, where he finds them more interesting because the customs differ so sharply — an interest that produced [Remains of the Day](/wiki/remains-of-the-day-book) and [Whispers in the Dirt](/wiki/whispers-in-the-dirt-book).<Cite t="1:32:06" /><Cite t="1:32:38" />
